options.C: They dictate the exact time of day nurses must count the inventory
options.D: They change the physical maximum storage capacity of the drug cupboard

explanation: Anticipating disease patterns allows the ward to stock up on relevant treatments before an outbreak or seasonal surge hits. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T14#GNS122_U3_T14_h5)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for the milk ejection or let-down reflex?

options.A: Prolactin
options.B: Estrogen
options.C: Progesterone
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Oxytocin makes the tiny muscles around the milk glands contract, squeezing the milk out into the ducts for the baby. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h2)

question: What is the biggest danger when an atherosclerotic plaque suddenly bursts open in a heart artery?

options.A: The heart rate slows down dramatically from nerve signals
options.B: The artery immediately widens and causes blood pressure to drop
options.C: A blood clot forms quickly over the break and blocks blood flow
options.D: Red blood cells leak directly into the chest cavity

explanation: When a plaque ruptures, the body treats it like an injury and forms a clot right there. Unfortunately, that clot can block the artery and cause a heart attack.

question: What is the main focus of critical care in the community setting?

options.A: Conducting clinical drug trials in large urban tertiary hospitals
options.B: Performing complex elective surgeries in rural primary health centers
options.C: Delivering life-saving interventions outside traditional hospital intensive care units
options.D: Managing chronic stable illnesses during routine home visits

explanation: You don't always need a big hospital ICU to save a life! Community critical care is all about bringing quick emergency help right to primary clinics and homes.

question: Which serious lung condition is a major emergency for a pregnant woman with sickle cell disease?

options.A: Placental abruption
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.C: Acute chest syndrome
options.D: Gestational diabetes

explanation: Spot on! Acute chest syndrome involves lung infection and tissue damage, bringing chest pain and fever that needs fast medical care.

question: A patient's waste moves through the colon at a normal speed, but they still struggle with hard stools and straining because of their diet. What do we call this type of constipation?

options.A: Slow-transit constipation
options.B: Normal-transit constipation
options.C: Mechanical bowel obstruction
options.D: Pelvic floor dysfunction

explanation: Even when the gut moves at a normal speed, everyday things like not eating enough fiber or drinking less water can cause normal-transit constipation. Easy peasy once you break it down!

question: What is a major ethical debate surrounding Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) like IVF?

options.A: Guaranteed elimination of all genetic diseases at birth
options.B: Compulsory fertility treatment for all citizens
options.C: Fair access and what to do with unused embryos
options.D: Total absence of any legal regulations worldwide

explanation: ART often raises tough questions about fairness in who can afford it and how leftover embryos should be handled ethically. [learn more](GNS216_U1_T8#GNS216_U1_T8_h6)

question: When handing over a critical patient, what does the acronym SBAR stand for?

options.A: Safety, Behavior, Analysis, Response
options.B: Symptoms, Blood pressure, Airway, Respiration
options.C: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
options.D: System, Burden, Action, Review

explanation: SBAR is your best friend for smooth handovers. Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation keeps everything short, sweet, and safe!

question: What is an important nursing duty after putting mydriatic eye drops in a patient's eyes for an exam?

options.A: Flush both eyes right away with normal saline
options.B: Keep them locked in a dark room for a whole day
options.C: Warn them about blurry vision and bright light sensitivity
options.D: Check their blood pressure every five minutes

explanation: Mydriatic drops widen the pupil and relax focusing muscles, making bright lights uncomfortable and vision blurry for a few hours.

question: What is the name of the muscular food pipe that connects your throat to your stomach?

options.A: Larynx
options.B: Pharynx
options.C: Trachea
options.D: Esophagus

explanation: Spot on! The esophagus is our dedicated highway for swallowing food down from the throat to the stomach.

question: Why is daily movement so important for patients who are stuck on bed rest?

options.A: It cures underlying chronic medical conditions completely
options.B: It prevents the loss of muscle strength and joint flexibility
options.C: It guarantees a shorter hospital stay for every patient
options.D: It eliminates the need for pain medication administration

explanation: Lying in bed all day makes the body weak very quickly. Simple daily movements stop muscles from wasting away and keep joints moving smoothly.

question: Why must a nurse maintain neutrality when counseling patients about genetic risks?

options.A: To allow patients to make their own choices based on personal values
options.B: To prevent patients from asking questions about their family
options.C: To prove that genetics has no real impact on health
options.D: To ensure the hospital avoids paying for laboratory tests

explanation: Reproductive decisions are deeply personal; nurses must guide without imposing personal beliefs or forcing specific choices. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h5)

question: A pregnancy is considered a normal term birth when delivery happens during which window?

options.A: Gestational age between 37 and 42 weeks
options.B: Induced contractions starting before 36 weeks
options.C: Breech presentation with a single fetus
options.D: Twin gestation with vertex presentation

explanation: Spot on! A full-term pregnancy that is ready for normal labour usually falls between 37 and 42 completed weeks with one baby in a head-down position.

question: A patient is having a tonic-clonic seizure on the ward. What is the nurse's immediate priority?

options.A: Turn the patient onto their side and clear nearby hazards
options.B: Restrain the arms and legs tightly to stop the shaking
options.C: Leave the bedside immediately to find the doctor
options.D: Force a padded tongue depressor firmly between the teeth

explanation: Safety first! Never hold them down or jam things in their mouth. Roll them gently onto their side to keep the airway clear and move sharp objects away.

question: What do we call the emotional exhaustion and burnout nurses feel after constantly caring for trauma and disaster victims?

options.A: Acute physical shock
options.B: Developmental regression
options.C: Somatic conversion
options.D: Compassion fatigue

explanation: Spot on! Compassion fatigue happens when caring for others day in and day out drains your own emotional tank. Always remember to care for yourself, too!

question: Which type of medication is commonly prescribed to ease painful muscle stiffness and spasms?

options.A: Antibiotics
options.B: Anticoagulants
options.C: Vitamins
options.D: Muscle relaxants

explanation: Muscle relaxants help reduce spasticity and the painful cramping associated with progressive neurological damage. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T15#GNS222_U4_T15_h4)

question: How do you check for pain in a critical care patient who is intubated and unable to speak?

options.A: By asking family members how much pain is present
options.B: By assuming intubated patients cannot feel pain
options.C: By waiting until the patient's blood pressure drops
options.D: By observing facial expressions and muscle tension

explanation: When words aren't an option, watch their body! Frowning, tense muscles, and restlessness tell a clear story.

question: What is the primary purpose of bilateral tubal ligation?

options.A: Permanent female contraception
options.B: Treatment for severe pelvic infections
options.C: Prevention of ovarian hormone production
options.D: Regulation of irregular menstrual cycles

explanation: Tubal ligation is specifically designed as a permanent surgical method to prevent pregnancy by blocking the fallopian tubes. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T019#GNS226_U6_T019_h1)

question: How should a patient lie during a standard percutaneous liver biopsy?

options.A: On their left side with knees pulled up
options.B: Flat on their back with their right hand placed behind their head
options.C: Sitting upright leaning over a bedside table
options.D: Flat on their stomach with arms stretched forward

explanation: Great job! This position opens up the right side of the chest wall, giving the doctor the best access to the liver.

question: Why might a doctor perform a therapeutic lumbar puncture?

options.A: To remove a kidney stone from the ureter
options.B: To check the patient's blood glucose level
options.C: To lower high pressure inside the skull
options.D: To clear an airway blockage in the lungs

explanation: You got it! Removing extra fluid during the procedure helps relieve dangerous pressure inside the skull when there is a fluid buildup.

question: Your patient looks nervous while you get ready to test their cranial nerves. What should you do first?

options.A: Proceed quickly with the exam to get it finished
options.B: Skip the neurological assessment entirely for the day
options.C: Administer a strong sedative medication immediately
options.D: Explain each step simply before performing it

explanation: Well done! Addressing your patient's worry with a gentle explanation builds trust and makes them feel much more comfortable.

question: Your clinic gets a donation of mosquito nets and supplements. Who should you give priority to?

options.A: Healthy young men in the local football club
options.B: Local political leaders and chiefs
options.C: Pregnant women and young children
options.D: Wealthy traders in the central market

explanation: Pregnant mums and young kids face the deadliest risks from malaria and poor nutrition, so they always come first.

question: What is the primary purpose of inserting an endotracheal tube?

options.A: To secure and maintain a patent airway
options.B: To measure systemic blood pressure continuously
options.C: To prevent the stomach from producing acid
options.D: To treat underlying lung infections directly

explanation: The main goal of endotracheal intubation is to keep the airway open and secure so oxygen can reach the lungs safely. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h1)

question: Which test gives the definitive, 100% confirmation of CJD?

options.A: Chest X-ray examination
options.B: Complete blood cell count
options.C: Neuropathological brain tissue exam
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid culture

explanation: You got it! While other tests help doctors look at clues, final confirmation requires checking brain tissue for those hallmark sponge-like changes.

question: When is the best time for a first follow-up visit after putting in an IUD (Intrauterine Device)?

options.A: After six months
options.B: After exactly five years
options.C: After twenty-four hours
options.D: After four to six weeks

explanation: Seeing the client at 4 to 6 weeks lets you check the IUD strings and make sure the device hasn't slipped out.

question: Which hormone directly stimulates the respiratory center to increase ventilation during pregnancy?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Progesterone
options.D: Estrogen

explanation: Progesterone acts directly on the brain's respiratory center, increasing the sensitivity to carbon dioxide and prompting deeper, more frequent breathing. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h2)

question: Which type of cholesterol is primarily responsible for plaque buildup in atherosclerosis?

options.A: High-density lipoprotein
options.B: Serum triglycerides
options.C: Low-density lipoprotein
options.D: Free fatty acids

explanation: Low-density lipoprotein, often called bad cholesterol, penetrates damaged artery walls and contributes directly to the fatty plaque. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T4#GNS213_U1_T4_h2)

question: What defines febrile neutropenia in a cancer patient?

options.A: High fever and high white blood cell count
options.B: Low red blood cells and high platelets
options.C: Fever and low white blood cell count
options.D: Normal temperature and low platelets

explanation: Febrile neutropenia is diagnosed when a patient has a fever alongside a dangerously low count of infection-fighting neutrophils. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is the main building block the body uses to make steroid hormones?

options.A: Glucose
options.B: Tyrosine
options.C: Cholesterol
options.D: Hemoglobin

explanation: Not all cholesterol is bad! Your body actually uses it as the foundational raw material to build important steroid hormones.

question: How are animal fats and oils usually used in traditional medicine?

options.A: As intravenous substitutes for blood plasma
options.B: As sterile eye drops for acute glaucoma
options.C: As primary replacements for oral antibiotics
options.D: As bases for topical balms and ointments

explanation: Animal fats make a nice, greasy base that helps carry healing ingredients and keeps them sticking to the skin to soothe pain or swelling.

question: Which hormone tells the Leydig cells in the testes to produce testosterone?

options.A: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone
options.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone
options.C: Luteinizing hormone
options.D: Thyroid-stimulating hormone

explanation: Spot on! Luteinizing hormone (LH) comes from the anterior pituitary gland and travels down to tell the Leydig cells to make testosterone. You've got this!

question: Which white blood cells are mainly responsible for making antibodies?

options.A: B-lymphocytes
options.B: Platelets
options.C: Red blood cells
options.D: Neutrophils

explanation: You nailed it! B-lymphocytes are the antibody factories of your immune system, churning out proteins that target specific invaders.

question: Why must patients with repaired heart defects take antibiotics before certain dental procedures?

options.A: To prevent infective endocarditis from bacteria entering the bloodstream
options.B: To lower their systemic blood pressure during the dental work
options.C: To keep their surgical chest incision from becoming dry
options.D: To prevent future heart rhythm changes after dental cleaning

explanation: Dental work can release bacteria into the blood. If it lands on repaired heart tissue, it can cause a serious infection called endocarditis. A dose of antibiotics keeps them safe!

question: You notice tidaling has suddenly stopped in the water seal chamber of a stable patient. What should you check first?

options.A: Check the tubing for kinks, blockages, or loops hanging too low
options.B: Call the surgeon to request immediate removal of the chest tube
options.C: Disconnect the drainage system from the wall suction source
options.D: Immediately clamp the chest tube with two heavy metal hemostats

explanation: Don't panic! When tidaling stops, it often just means something is blocking the tube, like a kink or a loop resting under the bed. Check the lines first.

question: A patient with acute diarrhoea has sore, red skin around their bottom. What is the best immediate nursing step?

options.A: Instruct the patient to avoid washing the area until stools stop
options.B: Gently clean the area, pat dry, and apply a barrier cream
options.C: Place a tight-fitting dressing over the skin to block moisture
options.D: Apply an alcohol-based wipe to disinfect the raw skin thoroughly

explanation: Frequent watery stools are very irritating to the skin. Keeping the area clean, dry, and protected with a good barrier cream is a nursing lifesaver for comfort and skin integrity.

question: What heart rate defines sinus tachycardia in an adult?

options.A: Less than 60 beats per minute
options.B: Greater than 100 beats per minute
options.C: Between 60 and 80 beats per minute
options.D: Between 40 and 60 beats per minute

explanation: Tachy means fast! Anything over 100 beats per minute coming from the sinus node is sinus tachycardia.

question: During a pelvic exam, a student nurse notices the lower uterine segment is wonderfully soft. What term goes in the clinical notes?

options.A: Goodell's sign
options.B: Hegar's sign
options.C: Quickening sign
options.D: Chadwick's sign

explanation: Hegar's sign specifically refers to the softening and compressibility of the lower uterine part felt early in pregnancy. You're mastering the terminology!

question: Which physical assessment finding is most characteristic of chronic motor nerve damage in the lower extremities?

options.A: Uncontrollable muscle expansion
options.B: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.C: Muscle atrophy and foot drop
options.D: Sudden involuntary limb sweating

explanation: When motor nerves stop stimulating leg muscles, the muscles shrink (atrophy), and the muscles lifting the front of the foot become too weak, leading to foot drop. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T18#GNS222_U3_T18_h4)

question: A patient with severe knee osteoarthritis gets no relief from oral pain relievers and physical therapy. What intervention is a nurse most likely to prepare the patient for next?

options.A: A complete blood transfusion
options.B: An intraarticular joint injection
options.C: Intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.D: An intramuscular vaccine dose

explanation: When conservative oral treatments fail for localized joint wear, doctors often step up to direct joint injections. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T9#GNS125_U3_T9_h3)

question: As a nurse, what is a crucial check to make *before* a patient goes for a liver biopsy?

options.A: Check that clotting blood tests are safe and consent is signed
options.B: Perform a minor surgery to drain belly fluid
options.C: Give them strong general anesthesia right in the ward
options.D: Make sure they eat a large heavy meal

explanation: Spot on! Safety first—always verify clotting labs and make sure the patient understands and signs the consent form before the procedure.

question: How does pursed-lip breathing help a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

options.A: It forces extra oxygen directly into the bloodstream through the mouth
options.B: It relaxes the stomach muscles to improve digestion
options.C: It stops the patient from coughing up thick mucus plugs
options.D: It slows down exhalation and keeps airways open longer

explanation: Pursed-lip breathing creates back-pressure in the airways, preventing them from collapsing too early and helping trap less air in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a core ethical principle guiding palliative nursing care?

options.A: Autonomy
options.B: Beneficence
options.C: Punitive dominance
options.D: Non-maleficence

explanation: Punitive dominance is made up! Nursing ethics are built on principles like autonomy, beneficence, and non-maleficence. Easy point for you!

question: A patient lies quietly with closed eyes, but opens them right away when you call their name loudly. What is their eye score?
explanation: Spot on! When they open their eyes only after you speak to them or call their name, that's a score of 3.

question: What drives the extremely fast skin cell growth seen in plaque psoriasis?

options.A: Cold weather triggers massive mast cell breakdown
options.B: The body attacks and destroys pigment cells in the base layer
options.C: Bacteria directly eat away at the outer skin layer
options.D: T-cells release chemical signals that speed up skin cell division

explanation: In psoriasis, hyperactive T-cells release inflammatory chemicals that tell skin cells to multiply way too fast, piling up into those thick, silvery scales.

question: What happened when major scandals broke out about ships dumping toxic waste?

options.A: They forced world leaders to create a binding international waste treaty
options.B: They led to a complete ban on all maritime shipping worldwide
options.C: They encouraged developing nations to build more local incinerators
options.D: They proved that ocean water naturally neutralizes heavy metal toxins

explanation: Well done! When media and the public saw wandering ships dumping dangerous cargo, world leaders realized they had to step in with strict international rules.

question: Why do nurses check routine blood tests for medical-surgical patients?

options.A: To replace the need for physical head-to-toe assessments
options.B: To permanently cure chronic underlying disease processes
options.C: To measure the exact total volume of blood in the body
options.D: To monitor physiological shifts and evaluate organ function

explanation: Blood tests are like a window into the body! They give you clear clues on how well internal organs are coping, helping you track your patient's recovery day by day.

question: What symptom does a patient classically feel during an aortic dissection?

options.A: A dull, aching pain in the calf muscle while walking
options.B: Sudden, severe tearing or ripping pain in the chest or back
options.C: Numbness and color changes in fingers during cold weather
options.D: Swelling and brownish discoloration around the ankles

explanation: An aortic dissection is terrifying because the inner layer of the aorta actually tears open, letting blood tunnel between the layers of the wall. Patients describe it as a violent 'ripping' sensation.

question: What is an important long-term instruction for a patient who just received a mechanical heart valve?

options.A: Never drinking pure water again
options.B: Avoiding all forms of physical movement forever
options.C: Stopping daily blood pressure checks at home
options.D: The need for lifelong anticoagulation therapy

explanation: Blood loves to stick to artificial surfaces! Patients with mechanical valves must take blood thinners (anticoagulants) for the rest of their lives to prevent dangerous clots.

question: Which lab test is most commonly used to find Chlamydia and Gonorrhea in men quickly and accurately?

options.A: Complete Blood Count with differential
options.B: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate
options.C: Basic metabolic electrolyte panel
options.D: Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT)

explanation: NAAT is the gold standard! It's super sensitive and can even be done using a simple urine sample.

question: What is finger clubbing typically associated with in chronic conditions?

options.A: Rapid dehydration from fever
options.B: Sudden bacterial throat infections
options.C: Long-term low oxygen levels in the blood
options.D: A temporary lack of dietary vitamins

explanation: Finger clubbing develops gradually as a result of chronic hypoxia and tissue changes in the extremities. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary clinical goal of performing debridement on a chronic wound?

options.A: To eliminate the need for proper patient nutrition and hydration
options.B: To completely seal the wound shut without needing any sutures
options.C: To stop all blood circulation directly underneath the skin surface
options.D: To remove dead tissue and encourage healthy new cell growth

explanation: Necrotic or dead tissue acts as a barrier to healing and a breeding ground for bacteria; removing it lets healthy granulation tissue form. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h4)

question: A patient with an untreated collapsed lung (pneumothorax) is booked for a flight. What should be done first?

options.A: Decompress or treat the condition before takeoff
options.B: Fly at a much higher altitude to cure the air pocket
options.C: Remove all supplemental oxygen from the patient
options.D: Proceed with immediate takeoff without any changes

explanation: You nailed it! Remember Boyle's law? Trapped air expands as you go higher, so a pneumothorax must be treated *before* takeoff to prevent a life-threatening crisis.

question: Which nursing diagnosis focuses directly on blood supply to the brain tissue?

options.A: Risk for Impaired Skin Integrity
options.B: Ineffective Tissue Perfusion (Cerebral)
options.C: Impaired Physical Mobility
options.D: Ineffective Airway Clearance

explanation: You've got this! This diagnosis simply points to situations where blood and oxygen aren't reaching brain cells properly because of swelling, clots, or bleeding.

question: What is the main thing you do during the evaluation phase of the nursing process?

options.A: Gathering initial demographic data during the patient's admission
options.B: Writing out shift handoff notes without checking patient progress
options.C: Comparing the patient's actual health status against the expected outcomes
options.D: Formulating brand new medical diagnoses for the physician to sign

explanation: Evaluation is like checking your scorecard. You look back at the goals you set and ask, 'Did our care help the patient reach them?'

question: How do disease-causing prions spread and multiply inside the brain?

options.A: By forcing normal proteins to change shape
options.B: By dividing rapidly through simple cell fission
options.C: By absorbing nutrients from nearby blood vessels
options.D: By replicating their own viral RNA strands

explanation: Spot on! Prions don't reproduce like normal germs; instead, they act like bullies, forcing healthy proteins to fold into the abnormal shape just like them.

question: Which piece of patient history helps you spot a potential idiosyncratic reaction?

options.A: Family history of unusual drug reactions
options.B: Current dietary preferences and fluid intake
options.C: Total daily fluid output measured in hours
options.D: Recent history of seasonal pollen allergies

explanation: Since these reactions often run in families due to genetics, asking about close relatives is a great nursing move. Keep it up!

question: What is a major risk when patients mix herbal remedies with prescription drugs?

options.A: Unpredictable interactions can cause severe bleeding or organ damage
options.B: Herbs neutralize all chemical side effects of modern medicine
options.C: Herbal remedies always cure diseases faster than prescriptions
options.D: Prescription drugs become completely odorless inside the body

explanation: Active compounds in herbs can clash with prescriptions, leading to dangerous complications. Always screen for local remedies!

question: A patient has been on strict bed rest for several weeks. What is likely happening to their bones?

options.A: Calcium storage in the bones is doubling
options.B: Bone-building cells are rapidly making the bones thicker
options.C: Bone breakdown (resorption) is happening faster than bone building
options.D: Spongy bone is turning into solid metal-like columns

explanation: Bones love movement and weight! Without that daily mechanical stress, the bone-builders slow down, letting the breakdown cells take over and weaken the bone density.

question: A patient on bedrest after hip surgery suddenly complains of chest pain and shortness of breath. What should you suspect?

options.A: Compartment syndrome
options.B: Pulmonary embolism
options.C: Hypovolemic shock
options.D: Fat embolism syndrome

explanation: Sudden breathlessness and chest pain in someone who has been immobile scream 'pulmonary embolism.' Quick assessment and action can save a life here!

question: A patient recovering from a leg fracture is frustrated and feels like giving up. Which rehabilitation goal addresses this?

options.A: Accelerating the bone fracture healing timeline
options.B: Eliminating the need for any future physical therapy
options.C: Promoting psychological adjustment and coping
options.D: Replacing lost joint cartilage with synthetic tissue

explanation: Recovery is tough mentally too! Supporting patients emotionally and helping them cope is just as important as the physical exercises.

question: What happens when alveolar macrophages try to swallow heavy loads of mineral dust?

options.A: They burst and release chemicals that cause scar tissue formation
options.B: They travel out of the lungs through the sweat glands
options.C: They turn into red blood cells to improve oxygen transport
options.D: They successfully dissolve the mineral dust into harmless sugar

explanation: When macrophages cannot digest toxic dust like silica, they break down and release inflammatory signals that trigger permanent lung fibrosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h2)

question: Why is checking blood sugar one of the first things to do when caring for an unresponsive patient?

options.A: Hypoglycemia is a metabolic cause of altered consciousness that can be quickly reversed
options.B: Glucose checks replace the need for a neurological exam
options.C: High blood sugar directly damages the brainstem within minutes
options.D: Diabetes mellitus is the primary cause of all neurological trauma

explanation: Spot on! Low blood sugar starves the brain of energy, causing unconsciousness that can fix itself almost instantly once glucose is given.

question: What happens to the baby's blood pressure right after the umbilical cord is clamped?

options.A: It remains completely unchanged
options.B: It drops down to zero
options.C: It fluctuates wildly every second
options.D: It increases significantly

explanation: You're doing awesome! Cutting the cord removes the low-resistance placenta, which causes an immediate rise in the baby's blood pressure. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h6)

question: What is your very first priority action if you suspect a patient is having an idiosyncratic drug reaction?

options.A: Wait for laboratory confirmation before acting
options.B: Increase the drug dose to build up a tolerance
options.C: Give the patient a strong dose of antihistamines
options.D: Stop the offending medication immediately

explanation: Rule number one of drug safety: if a medication is causing harm, stop giving it right away to protect your patient from further injury!

question: Why must a nurse sign or initial every entry made on a stock card?

options.A: To calculate the monthly salary bonus due to the nursing unit
options.B: To prevent the pharmacy department from reducing future supplies
options.C: To prove that the nurse worked extra hours on that specific day
options.D: To ensure accountability and provide a clear trail for audits

explanation: Signatures establish personal responsibility for every movement of stock, which is essential for investigating discrepancies later. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T14#GNS122_U3_T14_h2)

question: A patient complains that constant hospital noise and glaring overhead lights won't let them sleep. What kind of stressor is this?

options.A: Environmental stressor
options.B: Eustress
options.C: Psychosocial stressor
options.D: Physiological stressor

explanation: Things around us in our physical surroundings—like annoying hospital sounds or bright lights—are environmental stressors. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T15#GNS123_U3_T15_h3)

question: What does the FIFO stock rotation rule stand for?

options.A: Free-Issue, Fixed-Order
options.B: Final-Inspection, First-Order
options.C: First-In, First-Out
options.D: Fast-Item, Fast-Out

explanation: FIFO means the items that arrived first on the shelf should be the ones picked and used first. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T19#GNS122_U3_T19_h3)

question: Where is the best spot on the finger to prick for a blood sample?

options.A: The direct center of the finger pad
options.B: The base of the fingernail bed
options.C: The soft skin right over the joint
options.D: The side of the fingertip

explanation: The sides of our fingertips have fewer nerve endings than the pads, making the prick much less painful for your patient.

question: Why is it important to ask a patient about their current medications during a neuro history?

options.A: Medications completely cure all neurological disorders
options.B: Many drugs can alter mental status or cause tremors
options.C: Pharmaceutical records replace physical examinations
options.D: Drugs are the only cause of sudden vision loss

explanation: Certain drugs and everyday meds can make a patient feel confused or cause shaky hands, which can easily look like a brain problem if you don't check their drug history.

question: What is the main reason an indwelling catheter is left in place after fistula surgery?

options.A: To deliver strong liquid antibiotics directly into the kidneys
options.B: To flush out remaining blood clots from the abdominal cavity
options.C: To keep the bladder empty and prevent pressure on the repair site
options.D: To measure the patient's exact blood pressure every hour

explanation: You're right! Keeping the bladder deflated allows the newly stitched tissue to heal peacefully without stretching. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T12#GNS216_U5_T12_h5)

question: How does using the 'plate method' help patients manage their meals?

options.A: It provides a simple visual guide for portion control and food groups
options.B: It calculates the exact chemical calorie count of every single meal
options.C: It replaces the need for any further nursing follow-up or assessment
options.D: It legally restricts how much food restaurants can serve customers

options.A: Non-rebreather mask
options.B: Standard nasal cannula
options.C: Simple face mask
options.D: Venturi mask

explanation: The Venturi mask uses interchangeable adapters to mix exact amounts of room air with oxygen, delivering a very specific percentage of gas. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h3)

question: What is your main priority as a nurse right after skeletal traction is removed?

options.A: Supporting the limb carefully to prevent sudden pain or injury
options.B: Removing the patient's compression stockings and bed rest orders
options.C: Discharging the patient home immediately
options.D: Scrubbing the old pin sites with strong iodine to remove all scars

explanation: Brilliant! Once the traction is gone, the limb is unsupported and vulnerable. Always handle the limb with extra care to keep the patient safe and comfortable.

question: Which of these is NOT a common financial or social barrier to healthcare access in Nigeria?

options.A: High out-of-pocket expenses for routine medications and blood tests
options.B: Financial strain caused by the loss of daily income during hospital admissions
options.C: Free and unlimited universal healthcare coverage for all citizens
options.D: Long travel distances from rural villages to tertiary teaching hospitals

explanation: If only! Sadly, free universal healthcare isn't the reality yet, meaning out-of-pocket costs remain a huge hurdle for many patients.

question: A family caregiver is overwhelmed because their relative with memory loss keeps missing doses and mixing up pill times. What is the most helpful nursing intervention?

options.A: Tell the caregiver to stop giving all medications immediately
options.B: Warn them that missing doses has zero effect on chronic illnesses
options.C: Advise them to let the patient manage everything independently
options.D: Suggest practical tools like a labeled pill organizer and a daily schedule

explanation: Brilliant nursing advice! Simple organizational tools like pill boxes, alarms, and visual charts can lift a huge weight off family caregivers and keep patients safe on their medication routine.

question: Why does blood from an upper GI bleed usually turn black and tarry (melena) by the time it comes out?

options.A: The patient has been eating too many dark green vegetables
options.B: Bile acids in the large bowel bleach the blood
options.C: Stomach bacteria turn the iron bright red
options.D: Digestive enzymes and stomach acid break down the blood during its trip

explanation: As old blood travels all the way down the long digestive tract, stomach acid and enzymes break down the hemoglobin, turning it dark, sticky, and black.

question: A village has no local markets, poor farming land, and high unemployment. What health issue is most likely to spike here?

options.A: Stress-related injuries from high-speed driving
options.B: Malnutrition and poverty-related illnesses
options.C: Occupational hazards from heavy factory work
options.D: Complications from cosmetic plastic surgeries

explanation: Exactly. When the local economy struggles and people can't get basic food or income, malnutrition and poverty-related health issues naturally follow.

question: What is the most common cause of anaemia among pregnant women in Nigeria?

options.A: Rapid bone marrow aging
options.B: Not getting enough iron and folate in food
options.C: White blood cells destroying each other
options.D: Drinking too much water daily

explanation: Dietary gaps combined with the high demands of pregnancy are the top reasons for this. Good nutrition education changes lives!

question: Why are older adults at a higher risk of becoming dehydrated?

options.A: Their kidneys retain excess water automatically
options.B: They experience a blunted thirst response
options.C: They have an increased sense of thirst
options.D: Their body mass contains more water than younger adults

explanation: Older adults often don't feel thirsty even when their bodies are low on water because their natural thirst signals get weaker with age. Always encourage fluids!

question: What does 'apoptosis' mean when talking about nerve cell damage?

options.A: The blocking of blood vessels
options.B: The sudden growth of new neurons
options.C: The rapid repair of damaged myelin
options.D: The programmed death of cells

explanation: Apoptosis is simply the body's natural process of programmed cell death that happens when neurons get too stressed or damaged. Don't let big medical terms scare you—you're learning them step by step!

question: A patient is diagnosed with pseudogout. Which crystals cause this condition?

options.A: Calcium pyrophosphate
options.B: Monosodium urate
options.C: Calcium oxalate
options.D: Hydroxyapatite

explanation: Good to know! While regular gout is uric acid, pseudogout gets its name because it's caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals instead.

question: Why might an MRI or ultrasound be ordered for a patient with a rectovaginal fistula?

options.A: To check for active urinary tract infections
options.B: To test the patient's liver enzymes and kidney function
options.C: To evaluate the condition of the sphincter muscles and surrounding deep tissues
options.D: To measure the patient's daily fluid intake and output

explanation: Advanced imaging helps surgeons see the exact path of the fistula and check if the anal sphincter muscles are also injured. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T13#GNS216_U5_T13_h5)

question: What is a major risk of trusting pulse oximetry all by itself during a respiratory check?

options.A: Oxygen readings change too slowly to be useful
options.B: Oxygen levels can look fine while carbon dioxide is dangerously high
options.C: Pulse oximeters cannot measure heart rate accurately
options.D: High oxygen readings mean the patient is completely cured

explanation: A great oxygen saturation score doesn't mean they are blowing off carbon dioxide well. Always look at the whole patient!

question: Where are community health nurses most likely to first spot signs of giftedness or related stress?

options.A: Routine health screenings and immunization clinics
options.B: Emergency department trauma admissions
options.C: Surgical recovery and post-operative wards
options.D: Inpatient psychiatric stabilization units

explanation: Think about where we see children regularly before school problems start—during routine wellness visits and immunizations! You're thinking like a real public health nurse.

question: What happens at the cellular level right when a seizure starts?

options.A: Excessive neuronal excitation combined with a failure of inhibition
options.B: Massive overproduction of cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles
options.C: Rapid destruction of myelin sheaths along peripheral nerves
options.D: Complete depletion of glucose stores within glial cells

explanation: Seizures happen when brain signals become too excited and the brain's natural 'brakes' (inhibition) fail to slow them down. You are building strong clinical instincts!

question: Which of these is NOT a common risk factor for stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Obesity and excess body weight
options.B: Menopause and decreased estrogen levels
options.C: Frequent high-fluid intake throughout the day
options.D: Vaginal childbirth and multiple pregnancies

explanation: Drinking plenty of water is healthy! The real risk factors involve things that weaken pelvic support, like childbirth, hormonal shifts, or heavy pressure.

question: When lifestyle changes don't quite cut it, what type of medication is usually recommended first for pregnancy heartburn?

options.A: Heavy narcotic pain relievers
options.B: Prescription laxatives
options.C: Strong proton pump inhibitors
options.D: Antacids containing calcium or magnesium

explanation: Calcium and magnesium antacids work fast to neutralize acid and have a safe track record during pregnancy.

question: Why must patients take their antiretroviral drugs every single day without skipping?

options.A: The drugs degrade rapidly in the bloodstream if not replenished every hour.
options.B: Missing a single pill causes immediate permanent kidney failure in all patients.
options.C: Inconsistent medication intake can cause the virus to mutate and develop drug resistance.
options.D: Incomplete dosing causes the body to stop producing natural white blood cells.

explanation: Skipping doses gives the virus a chance to fight back and build resistance against the medicine. Adherence is key!

question: Why is a hollow-bore needle (like the ones used to draw blood) so dangerous if you accidentally prick yourself with it?

options.A: Hollow-bore needles often trap residual blood inside, increasing pathogen transfer
options.B: The plastic barrel attached to the needle releases toxic gas
options.C: Puncture wounds from needles never heal without surgical stitches
options.D: Needles used for drawing blood contain paralyzing chemicals

explanation: You nailed it. Because they are hollow, they act like tiny storage tubes carrying a good drop of infected blood right past your skin barrier.

question: Why must you never leave a set-up sterile field unattended on the ward?

options.A: Because sterile drapes automatically fold up after five minutes
options.B: Because the sterile items will melt if exposed to room air
options.C: Because someone might contaminate it without your knowledge
options.D: Because hospital regulations fine nurses who walk away from trays

explanation: Spot on! If you walk away, someone might unknowingly brush against it or contaminate it, ruining your sterile setup. Stay close to your work!

question: A pregnant woman arrives at a clinic bleeding heavily, but the nurses cannot help because there is no blood or oxygen. Which delay is this?

options.A: First delay
options.B: Community delay
options.C: Third delay
options.D: Second delay

explanation: That's the third delay! It happens when the patient finally reaches the health facility, but the facility fails to provide adequate, quality care due to lack of supplies or staff.

question: What is your very first action if a patient's chest tube accidentally disconnects from the drainage unit?

options.A: Apply tight adhesive tape all around the open tubing end
options.B: Clamp the chest tube securely near the insertion site
options.C: Submerge the end of the tube in sterile water
options.D: Lower the patient flat onto their back in bed

explanation: Quick thinking! Putting the tube tip in sterile water instantly creates a temporary seal and keeps air from rushing into the chest.

question: What is a practical way for a hospital to handle language barriers with patients?

options.A: Using written English pamphlets exclusively for all health education
options.B: Refusing admission to anyone who does not speak the official language
options.C: Providing translation services or multilingual staff members
options.D: Requiring all patients to learn medical terminology before booking an appointment

explanation: Spot on! Having translators or staff who speak local languages helps patients fully understand their care.

question: Which extrapyramidal side effect looks and acts almost identical to natural Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Pseudoparkinsonism
options.B: Tardive dyskinesia
options.C: Acute dystonia
options.D: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

explanation: 'Pseudo' means fake! Pseudoparkinsonism gives patients tremors, muscle stiffness, and a shuffling walk that looks just like Parkinson's, but it's actually caused by the medication.

question: What is the most important thing a nurse should do right after measuring vital signs?

options.A: Document the values promptly and accurately in the patient record
options.B: Memorize the numbers to tell the next shift verbally
options.C: Wait until the end of the shift to write everything down
options.D: Throw away the scrap paper to keep things clean

explanation: Exactly! Quick documentation ensures the whole healthcare team has up-to-date information to keep the patient safe.

question: What is the main goal of safe motherhood programs?

options.A: To shorten the duration of pregnancy
options.B: To reduce maternal and neonatal deaths
options.C: To promote exclusive formula feeding
options.D: To completely eliminate normal labor pain

explanation: Spot on! Safe motherhood programs are all about keeping both mothers and newborns safe, healthy, and alive. You've got this!

question: How should public health nurses view addiction when counselling patients?

options.A: As a permanent moral failure of the individual
options.B: As a condition cured strictly by financial fines
options.C: As a complex health condition requiring support
options.D: As a minor habit that requires no intervention

explanation: Correct! Seeing addiction as a health challenge rather than a moral failing makes patients feel safe to seek help without being judged.

question: What is the job of the thermopile inside an infrared thermometer?

options.A: It blocks bright room light from entering
options.B: It warms up the lens to match body heat
options.C: It pumps cool air over the computer chips
options.D: It converts absorbed heat into an electrical signal

explanation: Think of the thermopile as a translator: it takes the focused heat energy and turns it into an electrical voltage that the thermometer's screen can read.

question: How do re-emerging infectious diseases differ from emerging ones?

options.A: Re-emerging diseases are caused strictly by genetic mutations
options.B: Re-emerging diseases were previously declining but are now returning
options.C: Re-emerging diseases cannot be treated with standard medications
options.D: Re-emerging diseases only affect animals rather than human beings

explanation: Re-known diseases that had dropped in numbers come back to threaten populations, which defines the re-emerging category. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h1)

question: How long should a patient keep their fresh biopsy bandage clean, dry, and in place?

options.A: 5 to 7 full days
options.B: Until stitches fall out
options.C: 24 to 48 hours
options.D: At least two weeks

explanation: Leaving the first bandage on for 24 to 48 hours gives the skin a chance to start forming its natural protective seal against germs.

question: Why must instrument box locks and ratchets be kept open during the sterilization process?

options.A: To make it easier to count them after the cycle
options.B: To allow steam to reach all hidden surfaces
options.C: To make the instrument tray look neat and tidy
options.D: To prevent the metal handles from melting

explanation: Keeping hinges and box locks open ensures that the sterilizing steam makes full contact with every part of the metal. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T9#GNS123_U5_T9_h8)

question: What structure chemically connects the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary gland?

options.A: A specialized portal blood vessel system
options.B: Direct lymphatic drainage channels
options.C: The cerebrospinal fluid ventricles
options.D: Direct unmyelinated nerve fiber tracks

explanation: The hypothalamus uses a dedicated mini-blood highway (a portal system) to send chemical messenger hormones straight to the anterior pituitary.

question: Why is colchicine sometimes given along with NSAIDs to treat pericarditis?

options.A: To dissolve existing blood clots inside the heart chambers
options.B: To destroy resistant bacterial strains in the bloodstream
options.C: To permanently lower the patient's resting heart rate
options.D: To help prevent future episodes of the condition from returning

explanation: Colchicine is a helpful anti-inflammatory medicine added to treatment to stop pericarditis from coming back to trouble the patient again.

question: What is the most accurate way for parents to measure liquid paracetamol doses for children at home?

options.A: Using a standard kitchen teaspoon
options.B: Based on the child's height and shoe size
options.C: Using the age written on the medicine bottle
options.D: Based on the child's current body weight

explanation: Well done! Dosing by weight is the safest way to make sure the child gets the right amount, since kids of the same age can differ a lot in size.

question: Which licensing requirement must a tele-nurse always meet when caring for remote clients?

options.A: Holding a valid license in the location where the patient is physically located
options.B: Having a license from any country as long as the nurse has a smartphone
options.C: Possessing a special international internet communication permit
options.D: Registering only with the hospital administration board

explanation: Regulatory bodies require nurses to be legally licensed in the specific jurisdiction where the patient receives the care. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h4)

question: What is a key post-procedure instruction for a patient who received intravenous contrast dye during an MRI?

options.A: Avoid eating solid foods for the rest of the day
options.B: Take a strong diuretic medication immediately
options.C: Remain on complete bed rest for the next 24 hours
options.D: Drink plenty of fluids to help flush the contrast out

explanation: Increasing fluid intake helps the kidneys clear the contrast agent safely from the body. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T12#GNS123_U2_T12_h6)

question: Why do doctors order an MRI when they suspect a neurodegenerative disease?

options.A: To directly count the number of living neurons
options.B: To cure abnormal protein accumulation
options.C: To visualize brain structures and rule out other causes
options.D: To measure electrical brain waves

explanation: An MRI gives a clear picture of the brain so doctors can check for things like strokes or tumors that might look like a degenerative disease. Smart nursing insight!

question: Which of these is a clear example of an unsafe injection habit?

options.A: Using a contaminated needle to enter a single-dose medication vial
options.B: Using a fresh, sterile needle and syringe for every single patient
options.C: Dropping a used syringe straight into a safety box
options.D: Cleaning the skin with an alcohol swab before the poke

explanation: Never use a needle that has touched a surface or a patient to draw more medicine. It contaminates the whole vial and puts the next person in danger.

question: What happens in the nervous system when an opioid binds to its receptor?

options.A: It forces the body to release high amounts of natural prostaglandins
options.B: It stimulates rapid electrical firing along nerve endings
options.C: It inhibits the transmission of pain signals to the brain
options.D: It speeds up the heart rate to increase oxygen delivery

explanation: Think of opioids as a roadblock: they stop pain messages from traveling up the nerves so your brain doesn't feel them as intensely.

question: Why are stool softeners commonly prescribed after rectovaginal fistula repair?

options.A: To increase the speed of food digestion in the stomach
options.B: To prevent straining that can disrupt the suture line
options.C: To increase blood flow to the lower limbs
options.D: To cure chronic urinary tract infections

explanation: Avoiding hard stools and straining protects the delicate surgical repairs from tension and tearing. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T13#GNS216_U5_T13_h8)

question: Why should nurses treat a patient's fear as a serious clinical issue?

options.A: It allows the nurse to discharge the patient much faster.
options.B: It removes the need to administer prescribed medications.
options.C: It helps the nurse deliver targeted and empathetic interventions.
options.D: It ensures the patient will never ask questions about surgery.

explanation: You got it! Acknowledging fear as a real medical concern lets us give patients the exact emotional and physical backup they need to heal.

question: What is a top clinical priority when caring for a patient mid-flight?

options.A: Adjusting the aircraft navigation controls
options.B: Maintaining airway security and hemodynamic stability
options.C: Serving meals and beverages to the transport crew
options.D: Completing billing forms before landing

explanation: Spot on, nurse! Keeping the airway clear and vital signs stable will always be your number one duty in any critical transport.

question: Why can long-term stress cause a surgical wound to take longer to heal?

options.A: Lack of sleep stops red blood cells from carrying oxygen
options.B: High adrenaline levels directly dissolve skin proteins
options.C: Sustained cortisol release suppresses immune function and inflammation
options.D: Increased blood flow to the skin destroys newly formed collagen

explanation: When cortisol stays high for too long, it slows down your immune system and the natural healing steps your body needs to close up a wound. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T15#GNS123_U3_T15_h4)
